questions.definition: The basic economic problem that resources are limited but wants are unlimited.
questions.clue: Leads to choices and opportunity cost.
questions.explanation: Scarcity means societies must decide how to allocate limited resources between competing uses.

questions.definition: The next best alternative given up when a choice is made.
questions.clue: The cost of choosing one option over another.
questions.explanation: Opportunity cost exists because resources are scarce and choosing one use means sacrificing another.

questions.definition: The quantity of a good or service consumers are willing and able to buy at a given price.
questions.explanation: Demand depends on factors such as price, income, tastes, substitutes, and complements.

questions.definition: The quantity of a good or service producers are willing and able to sell at a given price.
questions.explanation: Supply can change because of production costs, technology, taxes, subsidies, or the number of firms.

questions.definition: The price where quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.
questions.clue: The market clears at this price.
questions.explanation: At equilibrium there is no shortage or surplus, so market forces are balanced.

questions.definition: A sustained increase in the general price level of goods and services.
questions.explanation: Inflation means money buys less over time. It is often measured using a consumer price index.

questions.definition: People who are willing and able to work but do not have a job.
questions.clue: Can be caused by changes in demand or technology.
questions.explanation: Unemployment can reduce output and incomes, and governments often aim to keep it low.

questions.definition: The price of one currency in terms of another currency.
questions.explanation: If a currency appreciates, imports may become cheaper and exports may become more expensive for foreign buyers.

questions.definition: Money collected by the government from households and firms.
questions.explanation: Governments use tax revenue to fund public services and influence economic behaviour.

questions.definition: A payment from the government to reduce production costs or encourage consumption.
questions.explanation: Subsidies can lower prices and encourage output, but they also require government spending.

questions.definition: Focusing on producing a limited range of goods or tasks.
questions.explanation: Specialisation can raise productivity, but workers or countries may become dependent on fewer activities.

questions.definition: The total value of goods and services produced in an economy over a period of time.
questions.explanation: GDP is a common measure of economic output and is often used to compare economic growth.
